name: subject-descriptor
intent: Give every part of a system one credential-independent representation of the entity on whose behalf an operation is performed, so authorization, audit and domain code can ask who is acting and read that subject's security-relevant attributes without knowing which credential format proved it.
problem: Authentication arrives in many formats - password plus session cookie, OIDC/JWT, mTLS certificate, API key, Kerberos ticket, signed assertion - while every decision downstream only needs the same few facts: a stable identifier for the acting subject and its roles or attributes. Without a common representation each consumer parses the credential itself, or a raw token or user-record type is threaded through the layers: consumers are coupled to one mechanism, two layers can disagree about who the caller is, attributes are re-derived per component, and values that were never verified get treated as authenticated.
context: Systems that establish identity once at a trust boundary and consume it in many places afterwards, and that have (or expect to have) more than one authentication mechanism feeding the same authorization and domain logic: server-side request processing (filters, middleware, interceptors, handlers), enterprise applications in front of JAAS, an STS or an identity provider, and service meshes where mTLS, bearer tokens and session cookies meet.
benefits: One identity representation for every consumer: guards, audit code and domain services ask for the subject identifier or a named attribute and never see a credential format, so adding a mechanism means writing one converter instead of touching every decision site.

Mechanism change becomes local: swapping a session cookie for OIDC, adding a second authenticator for service-to-service calls or retiring a legacy identity stack changes only the code that creates the descriptor.

Attributes become addressable: roles, groups, tenant, authentication method and assurance level are read through one documented interface, so authorization rules stop re-deriving them from tokens, headers or user tables.

Testability: a policy can be exercised with a hand-built descriptor for any role or tenant without standing up the authentication stack, and the test cannot accidentally take the real credential path.
Audit and forensics get a stable actor: log records and security events name the same identifier the authorization decision used, including the acting-versus-impersonated distinction.
Cross-cutting concerns attach in one place: tenant scoping, step-up requirements or minimal-disclosure rules read the descriptor instead of re-inspecting the credential in every layer.
tradeoffs: Staleness: the descriptor is a snapshot of attributes taken when verification succeeded; roles, group memberships or tenant assignments that change - or are revoked - afterwards keep their old values unless the descriptor carries an expiry and the application re-resolves it.

Trust conflation: once attributes from different origins sit in one object, consumers lose the distinction between values the authenticator attested and values the subject or an intermediary merely asserted, unless provenance is recorded per attribute.

Leaky, growing attributes: the descriptor becomes an attractive place to read anything about the user, so business logic starts depending on attributes that were meant only for the authorization decision and the interface turns into the identity provider's whole data model.

Concentration of sensitive data: one object that is logged, serialized into sessions and passed around collects exactly the personal and security-relevant attributes attackers want, so it needs the same handling rules as credentials.

Mapping cost per mechanism: every credential type, and every identity store behind it, needs its own converter and attribute resolution; when one path bypasses the descriptor, the uniform abstraction silently forks into two competing identities.
Impersonation and delegation are ambiguous by default: a subject may act for another subject, and a single "the user" identity hides which of the two an authorization decision must evaluate.

participants.responsibility: The entity on whose behalf operations are performed - a person, a service, a device, or an anonymous caller; its identity may arrive through any credential mechanism.

Read-only value holding the subject's stable identifier plus the security-relevant attributes consumers need (roles or scopes, tenant, authentication method, assurance level); carries no credentials and no credential-format details.
The authentication boundary: verifies whichever credential arrived and assembles exactly one descriptor per operation, so all mechanism-specific code lives here and nowhere else.

Authoritative provider the creator consults for non-credential attributes - identity-provider claims, directory, role store, session record - and the place where freshness and revocation rules are applied.

Presents the descriptor through the interface an existing consumer expects (java.security.Principal, IPrincipal, a policy-engine subject context) without exposing the descriptor's own type or the credential behind it.
Guard, domain service or audit component that asks the descriptor who is acting and reads attributes; it never sees, stores or forwards a credential.

use_cases: A web API reached by several mechanisms at once - session cookie for the browser app, bearer token for mobile clients, mTLS for service-to-service calls - where every path ends in the same descriptor and controllers and policies are written once.

An enterprise application behind a JAAS login module, an STS or an identity provider: the validated authentication result is converted into the descriptor, which carries subject id, roles and tenant for downstream authorization and audit.
A multi-tenant SaaS where tenant membership and subject identity travel together, so repository-level guards enforce isolation by reading one attribute instead of trusting a request parameter.
Support and impersonation workflows: the descriptor records acting subject and impersonated subject separately, so audit names both while authorization evaluates the acting one.
An authorization engine or policy decision point that expects subject attributes as input: the descriptor is serialized into the policy request instead of the raw token.
Migrating off a legacy identity stack (JAAS, Windows identities, a homegrown user table) to OIDC: consumers are switched to the descriptor first, and the mechanism behind it is replaced second.

Java SE with JAAS: login modules of any type assemble one javax.security.auth.Subject holding the caller's Principals plus public/private credential sets, and application code running inside Subject.doAs authorizes from the principals without ever touching the ticket that logged the subject in.

An ASP.NET Core app with cookie, JWT-bearer and certificate handlers registered as separate authentication schemes: each handler turns its verified credential into the same ClaimsPrincipal on HttpContext.User, so [Authorize] and authorization policies inspect claims whichever scheme authenticated the request.

A Spring Security application combining form login, OAuth2/OIDC login and mTLS: every AuthenticationProvider emits the same authenticated Authentication object inside a SecurityContext held by the SecurityContextHolder, so @PreAuthorize rules and domain services read one subject shape for all mechanisms.
avoid_when: There is exactly one mechanism and the platform already hands consumers the identity they need (ASP.NET Core HttpContext.User, Vapor req.auth, Spring Authentication): use that principal directly; a second descriptor would only create a second source of truth.

The credential itself must travel onward - on-behalf-of calls, delegation, a downstream API that requires the user's own token: carry the token or a signed assertion, because a credential-free descriptor deliberately loses that artifact.
No application code ever asks who is acting because the decision happens outside the process (a gateway or sidecar authorizing on the raw token): describe the subject where the decision is made.
Identity must be re-verified with the authority at every decision (per-request token introspection): a cached descriptor is the wrong artifact, the token is.
A single-purpose process without an authentication boundary (CLI tool, batch job, library code) where the operating system already supplies the only identity and one call site reads it.
anti_patterns: Descriptor as a credential bag: the token, session blob or password material travels inside or next to the subject object, so every consumer can read it and it ends up in logs and traces.

Merging attested and self-asserted attributes: values from an unverified header, query parameter or unsigned claim land in the same attribute set as verified ones, and downstream code cannot tell them apart.
Mutable global identity: a process-wide "current subject" that any component may enrich or overwrite, so what a guard sees depends on which code ran first.

Fat descriptor: the object grows into the whole user record - profile, preferences, history - until authorization code depends on the user store and the descriptor is no longer a security abstraction.
Re-deriving identity in consumers: business code still parses the token or queries the user table to double-check the descriptor, reintroducing exactly the mechanism coupling the pattern removes.
Descriptor without evidence: a cached copy kept across session revocation or role changes with no expiry, no re-resolution and no way to tell how old it is.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: verification (how the subject proved itself), representation (who is acting) and decision (what may be done) are distinct responsibilities.
Information hiding: credentials and mechanism details stay behind the creator; consumers see only the identity facts they are entitled to read.
Single source of truth: exactly one descriptor per operation, written once at the boundary, so no path can invent a second identity.
Dependency inversion: consumers depend on the descriptor interface or its value type, never on a credential format or an identity-store record.
Least privilege and minimal disclosure: the descriptor carries the attributes consumers legitimately need and nothing else.
best_practices: Create exactly one descriptor per operation, immediately after verification succeeds, and treat it as read-only from that point on.
Key it by a stable, mechanism-independent identifier (issuer plus subject, or a platform id) rather than a username, email or display name that can change.
Record provenance per attribute - attested by the authenticator, resolved from a directory, or self-declared - so consumers can require verified values where it matters.
Keep credentials, tokens and password material out of the descriptor; when a downstream call needs the credential, pass it as a separate, explicitly named artifact.
Give the descriptor an expiry or validation time and re-resolve it when the session changes (renewal, revocation, role change); never cache it without a refresh rule.
Adapt the descriptor to the platform's principal interface instead of teaching every guard the descriptor type.
Model impersonation explicitly, with acting subject and impersonated subject as separate fields and a documented rule that authorization evaluates the acting one.
sources: The Open Group, Security Design Patterns, Technical Guide G031 (Blakley, Heath & the Open Group Security Forum, April 2004) - chapter 8.4 "Subject Descriptor" (p. 59): provide access to the security-relevant attributes of an entity on whose behalf operations are to be performed.

Schumacher, Fernandez-Buglioni, Hybertson, Buschmann & Sommerlad, Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering (Wiley 2006) - the security pattern catalog this row belongs to (identity, subject and context patterns).

Oracle, Java SE 21 API Specification - javax.security.auth.Subject (and the JAAS Reference Guide): the platform Subject groups an entity's Principals with public and private credential sets, with permissions governing each set - the namesake realization of this pattern. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/security/auth/Subject.html and https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-authentication-authorization-service-jaas-reference-guide.html

Microsoft Learn, Overview of ASP.NET Core Authentication: authentication handlers resolve the request's credential into a ClaimsPrincipal that authorization consumes - one principal object across cookie, bearer-token and certificate schemes. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authentication/?view=aspnetcore-10.0

Spring Security reference, Servlet Authentication Architecture: SecurityContextHolder / SecurityContext / Authentication separate 'who is acting' from the provider (form, OAuth2/OIDC, mTLS) that produced it. https://docs.spring.io/spring-security/reference/servlet/authentication/architecture.html

IETF RFC 8725, JSON Web Token Best Current Practices: why attributes taken from a token are only trustworthy after signature, issuer and audience validation - the verification the descriptor's creator owes its consumers. https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8725/
